paras: The killing of John Cain was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a white man, Dave Hancock, at Blackburn, Missouri, on November 6, 1888. According to the only report found, a Sweet Springs correspondence in the Lexington Intelligencer, the trouble grew out of a political discussion and Cain died instantly.

Blackburn was described as a town neighboring Sweet Springs, Missouri. The report ran in the week of the 1888 presidential election, on a page whose local items included election results and reports of Harrison's election.

In a dispatch dated Sweet Springs, November 7, the correspondent wrote that John Cain, "color ed[colored]," had been "shot and instantly killed yesterday" by Dave Hancock, "white." The only cause given was that the trouble grew out of a political discussion; the report did not say who began the quarrel or where in Blackburn it took place.
The report said nothing of Hancock's arrest, and no report of an inquest, charge or trial was found.

The Intelligencer printed the item on November 10 as a single sentence of local correspondence on its first page, without a headline or comment. It identified both men by race and gave the political discussion as the cause, then turned in the same paragraph to a stabbing in Sweet Springs, where a Black man named Lock Johnson was captured by a posse and narrowly escaped being lynched. No other newspaper report of the killing was found.

framing.detail: A one-sentence local item without headline or comment, giving races as 'color ed' and 'white', in the same paragraph as the Lock Johnson near-lynching report.
